segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, I would say I most commonly use open evidence. Gotcha. Mostly for… like… kind questions that I get that are a little… that don't have super clear… answers or questions about, like, side effects for a medication or something that I'm not as familiar with.
segments.rationale: The participant describes routine use of a specific AI tool for questions that lack clear answers and for medication side-effect questions outside their familiarity. This is framed as a practical use case rather than a criticism.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: sometimes I'll use it as well to… if there's certain… reports, like, that we get, like, for instance, we often get these very detailed pathology reports, and sometimes there's a lot of language in there that I don't fully understand. I will paste, like, that area of the report into open evidence for interpretation. And then sometimes I'll use it... if I'm considering, like, a plan for a [PATIENT]. I want to, like, validate what I'm thinking.
segments.rationale: The excerpt shows two concrete uses: interpreting difficult report language and checking a tentative plan. The participant positions AI as interpretive support and validation rather than a sole decision-maker.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think one positive was… in the pink report, I really enjoyed that it organized the references by strength of evidence, Just because I think my biggest, like, hesitancy is often around… While a lot of them give you references, wondering… like, what the actual strength of that reference is.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly praises evidence ordering by strength and links it to an existing concern about not knowing how strong cited references are. This grounds both a preference and a trust-related concern.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, yeah. One is just, like, an overall, like, hesitancy of, like, wondering where it's coming from... One is it can really be buried in there, and often find that, like, it's Making a statement based off of, like. one or two sentences that might be in that report, and not necessarily, like, the overall, findings from that report.
segments.rationale: The participant identifies a trust problem: uncertainty about information origin and concern that outputs may rely on isolated sentences instead of overall study findings. The criticism is directed at how evidence is sourced and interpreted.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: that one compared to the other reports... was really brief... It didn't really get into details of, like, nuances... And then the other thing was for the table. segments.rationale: The participant critiques the brief assessment and visually busy table, yet ultimately values the report once its evidence-ordering function becomes clear. This reflects tension between content value and presentation burden.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked the structure of the… the tables and the overall structure, so the yellow one. segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The red one was my least favorite. segments.rationale: The participant links excessive length to real-world unusability and reduced trust in the summary. They also object to unprompted material as filler that does not match the question asked.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The yellow one gave very definitive answers without, like. Recognizing some of the nuances, like the blue one did... segments.rationale: The participant values early communication of nuance and conditional guidance, but finds ambiguous labeling risky and confusing. Confidence improves when the degree of certainty is stated up front.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I would say... The structure of the… yellow report... the length was the best. pasted with the way that the blue one, like, the verbiage in the blue ones, I liked better. segments.rationale: The participant explicitly describes a preferred hybrid report combining structure, wording, and reference organization from different examples. This gives a direct design specification grounded in the participant's own comparisons.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think, like, overall summary statement at the beginning is, like, Very important... definitely the... evidence that it's using to support the answer and the quality of that evidence... conciseness is very important, because when you see, like, 3 or 4 pages, I decide, like, I don't even want to, like, read it at all... I would say one to two pages... when you ask a question, you can then follow up... I think giving all of it at once is a little too much.
segments.rationale: The participant names must-have elements: top summary, supporting evidence, and evidence quality. They also gives a practical length target and prefers a system that allows follow-up rather than overloading the first output.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I would say I think the most important thing... is any way that it can make... Clinical duties that are, like, outside of, like. Face-to-face interaction with [PATIENTS] more efficient... I think some of the focus has been on, like. heavily on, ways that it can make decisions for you, which I don't think is necessarily what... I think that's where a lot of the hesitancy comes from... it's more so better to have as, like, a utility to make your time more efficient.
segments.object_of_evaluation: role of AI in clinical workflow
segments.rationale: The participant emphasizes efficiency gains for non-face-to-face work as the most valuable role for AI, while expressing hesitation about AI taking over decisions. Acceptance is framed as higher when AI functions as a utility.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I do, I think, like, to an extent... I don't think it should be used to make, like. major medical decisions... But I think it's incredibly helpful for things like could this cause these side effects? Or, is the symptoms that the [PATIENT] is complaining about, could it possibly be related to the treatment... Or, things about the medications, or summarizing reports so that you can make a clinical decision?
segments.rationale: The participant draws a boundary between major decisions, which should remain clinician-made, and supportive tasks such as side-effect questions, medication issues, and summarizing information. The value lies in informing decisions rather than replacing them.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: one, like, very niche use of AI... is we use it… we do something called contouring... drawing structures on images to plan radiation, and AI has been used to, like, speed that process up, and… I think that's something that people have quickly adopted because... it's... speeding up a lot of time that you would otherwise use that feels more wasted.
segments.rationale: The participant gives a concrete example of AI adoption where it saves time on a task perceived as necessary but burdensome. The acceptance appears linked to speed and the ability to check the output.

analytic_memos.summary: The participant already uses AI in clinical workflow, but mainly for bounded support tasks rather than autonomous decision-making. They use it for unclear questions, medication side effects, interpreting dense report language, and validating their own thinking. Across the sample reports, the participant most values concise structure, an upfront summary, and explicit communication of nuance. Evidence presentation is central to their trust: they want references ordered by strength and want the quality of evidence made visible. At the same time, they are wary when sourcing is hard to trace or when the tool appears to overinterpret isolated sentences. Long reports are especially problematic because they reduce both usability and confidence, especially when the participant cannot review the underlying support. Overall, the participant favors AI as a utility that saves time and brings evidence forward, not as an agent that makes major clinical decisions on the clinician's behalf.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: The participant wants nuance, but still wants the report to be concise and quickly scannable.
They value conditional guidance, but only when it is labeled clearly enough to avoid misreading.
They appreciate rich evidence display, but busy formatting can hide the value of that content.
They see a role for AI in decision support, but resist AI being framed as the actual decision-maker.
